newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's falling share of production slammed.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's falling share of production slammed.

text.p: The sharp decline in South Africa's share of world production and the continued dominance of commodity exports came under fire in Boland Bank's latest economic review.
Boland Bank economist Francois Jansen said it was unacceptable that South Africa's share of world production had fallen to about 0.4 percent from about 0.7 percent in the 1980s.
"The challenge for South Africa lies in the manner in which the country addresses this unacceptable performance and its ability to compete on a par with the rest of the world," Jansen said.
He also criticised South Africa's reliance on commodities as its main exports.
Current world prices of most metals were at their lowest levels since May 1994 and were unlikely to show any significant recovery in 1997.

"In the long run, the worldwide shift towards new technologies and new materials will diminish the importance of traditional commodities, which are still contributing a staggering 60 percent to overall South African export earnings," Jansen said.
Jansen said these were some of the issues business should bear in mind as they prepared for 1997, which promised a mixed economic outlook.
Economic expansion in the U.S. was continuing, while there were encouraging signs in most other regions.
But economic recovery in most European countries, who were South Africa's main trading partners, was expected to be sluggish.
World inflation finally appeared to be under control and it remained important for South Africa to match inflation in its major trading partners to remain competitive.

While the depreciation of the rand against the dollar was making South African exports more competitive, the weakening of European and Asian currencies against the dollar would offset some of these benefits, Jansen said.
About 60 percent of South Africa's trade is priced in U.S. dollars.
At the same time, the lower rand made South Africa's imports more expensive but this could be offset by weaker European and Asian currencies, Jansen added.
